en: The Sūtra of the Questions of Śāntasvaravighuṣṭa, also known as the Sūtra on Purity and Subjugation Spoken by the Tathāgata, translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharma-hai of the Song Dynasty by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavat was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha.
He was accompanied by a great community of eight hundred bhikṣus, twelve thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and various devaputras from the desire realm, the form realm, and the Śuddhāvāsa heavens.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a respectful assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands who sat about him as he preached the Dharma.

Then, from within the assembly, there was a devaputra named Silent-Tuned-Voice (Śāntasvaranirghoṣa) who, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"Where is the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī now?
This great assembly, for the sake of hearing the Dharma, yearns with thirsting longing to behold that worthy gentleman."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāntasvarā:

"To the east, passing from here through ten thousand buddha-fields, there is a world named Ratnasthiti; the Buddha there is named Ratnalakṣaṇa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently resides there."
“Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, shall preach the Dharma to those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as is appropriate.
At that time, the devaputra Śāntamati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
I pray that you will manifest a subtle sign so that that worthy man may come to this assembly. Why is this?
World-Honored One!
Except for the Tathāgata, among all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, none are able to preach the Dharma as Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, does. Why is this?

By the power of the World-Honored One’s and Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta’s preaching of the Dharma, Māra found no opportunity; all the palaces of the Māras were made to vanish and remain unseen. He was able to subdue all the various heterodox teachers and those of wrong views; those with overweening pride were freed from their arrogance; those who had not yet resolved to attain Bodhicitta were led to generate that resolve; those who had already generated it attained non-retrogression; those who could be accepted were immediately accepted; and those who were not yet fit for acceptance were skillfully tamed, so that the Buddha’s True Dharma might long abide in the world.

At that time, having accepted the request of the devaputra Śāntasvaraghoṣa, the World-Honored One emitted a single ray of light from the mark of the white tuft between his eyebrows. This supreme radiance shone throughout the trichiliocosm; after penetrating and illuminating ten thousand buddha-fields, it shone everywhere across the world-system Ratnavyūha.
When those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas saw this light, they addressed the Buddha Ratnaketu, saying:
"What auspicious sign is this that causes a great light to shine universally throughout this world?"
That Buddha addressed them, saying:
"Sons of good family!

To the west, passing from here through ten thousand buddha-fields, there is a world named Sahā. There dwells a Tathāgata named Śākyamuni, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is currently preaching the Dharma."
"This is the light from the white tuft of hair emitted by that Tathāgata; having passed through ten thousand Buddha-fields, this light has come to illuminate this world.
Those bodhisattvas addressed their own Buddha, saying, "For what reason has the Tathāgata Śākyamuni emitted this radiance?"
That Buddha addressed the great assembly, saying:
"O sons of noble family!

Śākyamuni Tathāgata, together with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of bodhisattvas, Śakras, Brahmās, world-protectors, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, longs to see Mañjuśrī and hear his preaching of the Dharma out of a thirsting aspiration for the teaching. For this reason, that Buddha has emitted this radiance."
At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnaketu addressed the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, saying: "Good son,
go to the Sahā world."
"That Tathāgata Śākyamuni and the great assembly are waiting to see you and hear the Dharma you shall preach.
Then Mañjuśrī addressed that Buddha, saying,
"So be it, World-Honored One!"
"I have already seen the light.

At that time, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, together with ten thousand bodhisattvas, prostrated before that Buddha and circumambulated him three times to the right. Then, in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, he and the ten thousand bodhisattvas suddenly vanished from that world and arrived in the Sahā world, staying in mid-air. To make offerings to the Buddha, they rained down the most pure flowers; the fragrance of those flowers pervaded the entire assembly, accumulating up to the knees.
At that time, the great assembly marveled at what had never occurred before and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
By whose spiritual power were these wondrous flowers rained down? The Buddha told the great assembly:

"This is the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, together with ten thousand bodhisattvas, who have come from the world-system Ratnāvatī to this Sahā world; for the sake of making offerings to the Buddha, they are raining down these exquisite flowers from the sky above. The Devaputra Śāntasvarā addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
I wish and desire to see Mañjuśrī and that assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
World-Honored One!
That good man is a savior for those who have no savior.

Having spoken these words, Mañjuśrī the Dharma Prince, together with ten thousand bodhisattvas, suddenly descended from the sky above. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and circumambulated him seven times. Then Mañjuśrī sat upon a lion throne of lotuses manifested by his own power, and the ten thousand bodhisattvas likewise prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and circumambulated him seven times to the right. Standing before the World-Honored One with palms joined toward the Buddha, they spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!...”
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnākara respectfully inquires after the World-Honored One:
"Are you free from illness and affliction? Are your strength and vigor well?
When those bodhisattvas had finished speaking these words, they each sat upon seats manifested by their own power.
At that time, the Devaputra Silent and Well-Tuned Voice addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
This great assembly now thirsts with longing to hear the sublime Dharma spoken by the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī."
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me leave to ask a few questions.
The Buddha told the devaputra:
“Whatever doubts you may have, feel free to ask as you wish.”
Then, the Devaputra Śāntasvararāja, with a mind of reverence, addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"By what means does the Tathāgata Ratnaketu teach the Dharma in his world?"
"O Benevolent One, you delight in that. Mañjuśrī said, "O Devaputra!"

The Dharma he teaches is not for the sake of generating desire, nor for the sake of exhausting desire; it is not for the sake of generating hatred, nor for the sake of exhausting hatred; it is not for the sake of generating delusion, nor for the sake of exhausting delusion; it is not for the sake of generating afflictions, nor for the sake of exhausting afflictions.
"Why is this? Because, fundamentally, that which is without arising is without cessation.
The Celestial Son said:
“Mañjuśrī! Do the sentient beings in that land experience the arising and ceasing of the various fetters, such as desire and the rest? Mañjuśrī replied:
"So it is," the devaputra said. "If this is so, what is it that the Buddha’s teaching cuts off?"
Mañjuśrī said: "The Dharma is fundamentally unarisen; what could possibly be exhausted? Why is this so?"
In that Buddha-world, sentient beings have neither ignorance nor cessation, neither cultivation nor realization.
The sentient beings of that realm value the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) and do not value the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
The devaputra said:
“Mañjuśrī! What is the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya)?”
"What is the truth of skillful means? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Son of Heaven!..."

Meaning (artha) is not designated by way of arising, nor is it designated by way of destruction; it has no characteristic of location and no characteristic of non-location; it is neither a single characteristic nor the absence of characteristics; it has no characteristic of influence; it is neither characterizable nor uncharacterizable; it is neither exhaustible nor inexhaustible; it neither falls away nor does it not fall away—this is called the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya).
"O Son of Heaven!

The ultimate meaning is without mind and without the continuity of mind; it is not a track and not a non-track; it is not this shore, not the other shore, and not the middle stream. This is called the First Noble Truth."
That which is nameless and devoid of syllables is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Why is this so?
Because the World-Honored One has taught that all sounds are entirely false and illusory.
The devaputra said:
"Mañjuśrī! Is that which the World-Honored One has spoken also entirely false?"
Mañjuśrī said: “The World-Honored One speaks neither of reality nor of falsehood. Why is this? Because—”

The World-Honored One dwells apart from the two extremes, transcending mind, thought, and speech; within the realm of conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, he speaks neither of reality nor of unreality, and for this reason, there is non-duality.
"Son of Heaven!
What do you think? If a person created by the Tathāgata through his transformative power were to say something, would it be real or false?"
The devaputra said:
“Both are non-existent. Why is this so?
"The person emanated by the Tathāgata has no body and no accomplishment.
Mañjuśrī said: "So it is, O Devaputra!"
“The Tathāgata says that all dharmas are identical in nature to a magical transformation; he speaks neither of reality nor of unreality, and for this reason they are non-dual.
The devaputra said: “Mañjuśrī!...”
"How does the Tathāgata speak of the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya)? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Son of Heaven!"
The ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is ineffable. Why?
Because it is ineffable.
Why is this? Because it cannot be compared, cannot be spoken of, and cannot be named; this is called the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
When this ultimate truth was being taught, five hundred bhikṣus were freed from dust and removed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.
Two hundred devaputras attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). The devaputra Śānta-svara then asked Mañjuśrī:
"The ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is difficult to exhaustively fathom."
Mañjuśrī said: "It is so, O Devaputra!
The ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) is difficult for those who do not practice with correct diligence to fully exhaust."
The devaputra asked,
“What is the right diligence of a bodhisattva? Mañjuśrī replied:
"If a bodhisattva exerts diligence not for the sake of knowing, not for the sake of abandoning, not for the sake of cultivating, and not for the sake of realizing, this is called right diligence."

Why is this so? If one thinks, "This should be known," "This should be abandoned," "This should be cultivated," or "This should be realized," then that is a sign, that is grasping, that is conceptual proliferation, and that is conditioned activity.
"If one practices in this way, it is not called right effort.
The devaputra asked: "If that is so, then what is called right effort?"
Mañjuśrī said: "The equality of suchness and the equality of the dharma-realm are identical to the equality of non-hearing.
The equality of suchness and the equality of the dharma-realm are identical to the equality of seeing."

The dharmas of ordinary beings, the dharmas of those in training, and the dharmas of those beyond training; the dharmas of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas; these are identical to all conditioned phenomena, to nirvāṇa, to defilement, and to purity.
"One who possesses such impartial diligence is said to have right diligence. The devaputra said: "Mañjuśrī!..."
"What is the suchness that is equal to defilement and purity? Mañjuśrī replied,
"It is the suchness of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness."
Why is this? Because, O Son of Heaven, nirvāṇa is empty.
Just as the emptiness within an earthenware vessel and the emptiness within a precious vessel are neither two nor different, so it is, O Devaputra!
The emptiness of defilement and the emptiness of purity are both the same single emptiness; they are neither two nor different.
The devaputra said:
“Mañjuśrī, should a bodhisattva apply diligence toward the noble truths?”
Mañjuśrī said: “O Devaputra!
If a bodhisattva does not exert diligence regarding the various truths, how could he possibly preach the Dharma for the sake of śrāvakas?”
Why is this? When a bodhisattva cultivates the truths, there is necessarily a purpose; when a śrāvaka cultivates the truths, there is no such purpose.
When a bodhisattva cultivates the truths, they possess skillful means; when a śrāvaka cultivates the truths, they lack skillful means.
When Bodhisattvas cultivate the truths, they possess discernment; when Śrāvakas cultivate the truths, they lack discernment.
Bodhisattvas cultivate the truths for the sake of all sentient beings and do not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi);
Bodhisattvas cultivate the truths with firm skillful means and do not abandon the gates of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
"O Son of Heaven! A Bodhisattva cultivates the Truths for the sake of all Buddha-dharmas.
It is like a person who, separated from a great caravan leader, attempts to cross a vast wilderness alone; his mind is filled with terror, and he can only pass through with difficulty."
"O Son of Heaven!

It is the same with the śrāvaka: fearing birth and death, his mind harbors alarm and dread; he has no intention of returning to this world, nor does he possess the mind that acts for the sake of sentient beings. He contemplates birth and death as vast and remote, lacking skillful means regarding the Buddha-dharma, and practices the various truths alone and without a second."
"O Son of Heaven!
Just as that caravan leader, possessing abundant wealth and assets, has crossed the wilderness and extensively benefited sentient beings;
so it is, O Son of Heaven!"

The Bodhisattva is like a great caravan leader, fully endowed with great loving-kindness and great compassion; he has accomplished the benefit of the Dharma and is possessed of tranquility. Skillfully governing his assets through expedient means, he boards the ship of the six perfections and wields the bow and arrows of the four means of integration, perfecting his skillful means as he cultivates the various truths for the sake of the Buddha-dharma.
"Devaputra!
It is like a dog skin that has been perfumed with sumana, campaka, and vārṣika flowers; although it has been transformed into fragrance, it is not loved or enjoyed by any humans or devas."

The śrāvaka’s cultivation of the truths is likewise: with their vows unfulfilled, they attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state; they cannot produce the fragrance of extensive learning, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; nor can they sever the latent tendencies of afflictions; and thus they are not loved or cherished by humans or devas.
"O Son of Heaven!

It is like the celestial Kāśika cloth, which is constantly perfumed with hundreds of thousands of kinds of pure incense, such as tagara, agaru, candana, and bhadraśrī, and is thus cherished by all humans and devas."

The Bodhisattva is likewise thus: throughout hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he perfumes himself by practicing the Dharma of the Truths; during that interval, he does not enter parinirvāṇa, and with all his vows fulfilled, he is able extensively to produce the fragrance of the supreme, pure scents of much learning, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. Having severed the habitual tendencies of the afflictions upon which they depend, he is beloved by all humans, devas, asuras, and others.
The Devaputra Silent-Tuned-Voice (Śāntasvaranirghoṣa) again addressed the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, saying: "Mañjuśrī!
What are the virtuous qualities of the assembly of śrāvakas in that world-system of the Tathāgata Ratnākara?"
“O Benevolent One, you are able to share in that joy with them. Mañjuśrī said: “Those śrāvakas do not possess firm faith, yet they are not those who rely on the faith of others;

they do not possess firm dharma, yet they are not separate from the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). They are not ‘persons of the eight stages’ (aṣṭamaka), yet they have crossed over the eight wrong paths. They are not srotāpannas, yet they are free from the fear of all evil realms. They are not sakṛdāgāmins, yet for the sake of transforming sentient beings, they manifest coming and going. They are not anāgāmins, yet they have gone into the past of all dharmas. They are not arhats, yet they truly receive the offerings and gains of the trichiliocosm. They are not śrāvakas, yet they are able to understand and realize what all Buddhas have taught. They are not separated from the taints of desire, yet they are not scorched by the fire of desire; in places of grasping and attachment, they are free from all longing.”
Without being free from hatred, they are not afflicted by the torment of anger, nor do they give rise to resentment or obstruction toward any sentient being;
without being free from delusion, they are not obscured by ignorance, remaining free from all darkness regarding all phenomena;
and without being free from afflictions, they diligently strive to sever the afflictions of sentient beings.
Without ascending to the stage of certainty, they do not undergo rebirth; they transform and deliver sentient beings without the mark of self;
they fully repay the kindness of donors without any grasping or receiving; they cultivate the foundations of mindfulness without notions of gratitude or recollection;
they cultivate the right efforts without arising or ceasing; and they give rise to the bases of psychic power while remaining detached from body and mind, in order to fulfill [the perfections].
They cultivate the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) for the sake of fulfilling the spiritual faculties of all sentient beings;

they cultivate the various faculties (*indriya*) for the sake of increasing the roots of all sentient beings; they cultivate the various powers (*bala*) for the sake of destroying all afflictions (*kleśa*);
they cultivate the various factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) for the sake of awakening to the wisdom of equality; and they [cultivate them] for the sake of crossing over all deviant paths.
One cultivates the various paths in order to attain the Way and thereby realize the unconditioned; one cultivates the supernormal powers in order to enter the limit of reality;
one gives rise to knowledge and vision in order to enter the Dharma-realm; one gives rise to illumination in order to exhaust ignorance;
and one cultivates liberation in order to depart from the two extremes.

With the fleshly eye, they see all Buddhas and their worlds, as well as the sentient beings within those worlds; with the divine eye, they see the birth and death of all sentient beings; with the wisdom eye, they comprehend the mental activities of all sentient beings; with the Dharma eye, they perceive the equality of all phenomena and contemplate the equality of all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time; and with the Buddha eye, they illuminate the Buddha-dharma.

With the divine ear, they understand all that is spoken by the Buddhas; with a single mind, they know the mental activities of all sentient beings; with the wisdom of recollection, they remember the limits of past kalpas; with the power of spiritual travel, they pass through boundless Buddha-fields; and with all outflows extinguished, they attain liberation through the mind of non-arising.

Although they are visible, they do not establish a physical body; although there are written characters, there is no verbal discourse. Their minds are inconceivable and their speech is unimpeded; their countenances are upright and dignified, most pleasing to behold. They are adorned with all the marks and signs of excellence and the glory of merit; their majestic virtue is difficult to gaze upon, and their renown is lofty and far-reaching. Their essence is endowed with praise, yet they are unstained by worldly dharmas. They are not afflicted by the various troubles of the world nor defiled by evil words. They sport in the various supernormal powers, possessing great learning and ready eloquence. Their wisdom and insight leap forth with joy, extinguishing the darkness of ignorance. Their blazing wisdom allows them to preach the Dharma without hindrance; they have deeply entered the *dhāraṇīs* and are looked upon with care by all Buddhas.

This is not seen by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; their mindfulness is like the great ocean, their concentration is like Mount Sumeru, their endurance is like the earth, their supernormal transformations are like Indra, their mastery over the mind is comparable to Brahmā, and they are unequaled and equal to space, pervading all places and entering all realms.
“O Son of Heaven!
The virtues of the assembly of śrāvakas in the world of that Tathāgata Ratnākara are all such as these; furthermore, they have accomplished immeasurable merits.

When this Dharma was being taught, five hundred bhikṣus, five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, five hundred upāsakas, five hundred upāsikās, and five thousand sons of gods who had not yet attained the stage of certainty each spoke these words:
“We wish to go with joy to that land to join the assembly of śrāvakas of the Tathāgata Ratnākara. Mañjuśrī said,
“O sons of good family!...”
One cannot be born in that land with the mind of a śrāvaka.
Therefore, you all should resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; only then can you be born there.
At that time, the great assembly, desiring to be born there, gave rise to the aspiration for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* with the vow to be reborn in that land.
The World-Honored One then declared that they would indeed attain rebirth there.
The Devaputra Śāntasvaraghoṣa again addressed the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, saying: “Mañjuśrī!
By what dharmas does that land discipline the śrāvakas and discipline the bodhisattvas?”
Mañjuśrī said: “O Devaputra!

One takes on a body to discipline śrāvakas through the nature of the three vehicles, and to discipline bodhisattvas by comforting all sentient beings through the gathering of immeasurable births and deaths.”

They discipline śrāvakas by disparaging the accumulation of merit and resources, and they discipline bodhisattvas by not wearying of the vast accumulation of merit and resources for the benefit of sentient beings.

One who disciplines śrāvakas does so out of no desire to sever the afflictions of all sentient beings; one who disciplines bodhisattvas does so out of the aspiration to sever the afflictions of all sentient beings.

One who disciplines śrāvakas does so by relinquishing all sentient beings without seeking to accomplish all Buddha-dharmas; one who disciplines bodhisattvas does so with a heart of great compassion, mindful of all sentient beings, for the sake of accomplishing the dharmas of all Buddhas.
They discipline śrāvakas through practices that are limited in scope, and they discipline bodhisattvas through practices that pervade all worlds.
They discipline śrāvakas by abandoning the various māras, and they discipline bodhisattvas by terrifying the māras of all worlds and crushing opposing arguments.
One tames śrāvakas by means of accomplishing one's own mind; one tames bodhisattvas by means of accomplishing the unsurpassed bodhicitta.
One tames śrāvakas by means of illuminating oneself; one tames bodhisattvas by means of illuminating the bodies of all sentient beings in all worlds as well as the Buddha-dharma.
They discipline śrāvakas through the skillful means of gradual progression, and they discipline bodhisattvas through the skillful means of a single moment of mind.
They discipline śrāvakas by severing the lineage of the Three Jewels, and they discipline bodhisattvas by nurturing the lineage of the Three Jewels.
By repairing broken pottery and stone vessels, he tames the śrāvakas; by repairing broken gold and silver vessels, he tames the bodhisattvas.

By not accomplishing the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, he tames the śrāvakas; by accomplishing the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, he tames the bodhisattvas.

By means of not accomplishing the six pāramitās and the four saṃgrahavastus, they discipline śrāvakas; by means of accomplishing the six pāramitās and the four saṃgrahavastus, they discipline bodhisattvas.

They discipline śrāvakas by delighting in solitary dwelling in forest thickets and in seclusion; they discipline bodhisattvas by delighting in groves, parks, and pavilions, and by delighting in the joy of the Dharma.
They discipline śrāvakas by severing the habitual tendencies of afflictions; they discipline bodhisattvas by not severing the habitual tendencies of afflictions.
One tames śrāvakas through that which is measurable, conceivable, comparable, and numerable; one tames bodhisattvas through that which is immeasurable, inconceivable, incomparable, and innumerable.
"This is called subduing.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
You have well explained this taming of bodhisattvas.
Now listen as I speak a parable to further clarify this meaning, Mañjuśrī!
It is like this: suppose one person were to spend their entire life praising the water in a cow’s footprint, while another person praised the waters of the great ocean.
Mañjuśrī, what do you think?
“Can these two waters be compared to one another?
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"The footprint of an ox is very small, so its praise is also small;
the great ocean is immeasurable, so its praise is also immeasurable.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"It is so, Mañjuśrī! Just as the water in a cow's footprint is small and its praise is likewise small, so too is the discipline of the śrāvakas."
"Just as the waters of the great ocean are immeasurable and its praises are likewise immeasurable, so too is the taming of bodhisattvas.
When this Dharma was spoken, twelve thousand devaputras conceived the aspiration for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and said:
"World-Honored One!"
"We, too, wish to learn the bodhisattva’s discipline, so that we may discipline immeasurable sentient beings.
The Devaputra Silent Melody then addressed the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, saying, "Mañjuśrī!..."
“Virtuous one, what kind of discipline do you study?
Do you study the discipline of the śrāvakas, the discipline of the pratyekabuddhas, or the discipline of the bodhisattvas? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Son of Heaven! What do you think?
Is there any great ocean that does not receive the various streams?”
The devaputra said, "No. Mañjuśrī said:
"Thus it is, O Devaputra!

The taming of all bodhisattvas is like the great ocean; they apply themselves diligently to the skillful means of taming, cultivating the taming of śrāvakas, the taming of pratyekabuddhas, and the taming of bodhisattvas."
The devaputra said:
“Mañjuśrī! What is the meaning of the term ‘the phrase of subduing’?”
Mañjuśrī said: "If one knows the afflictions and cuts off the afflictions, this is called 'taming.
The devaputra said:
“Mañjuśrī! How does one subdue the afflictions?
How does one know the afflictions?”

Mañjuśrī said: "If one engages in false conceptualization, discrimination, and recollection, and does not practice skillful reflection; if one calculates the existence of self and other, and is entangled by views associated with annihilationism and eternalism, as well as by inversion, ignorance, and so forth—this is what constitutes being bound and attached by afflictions."

If one does not engage in false conceptualization, discrimination, or recollection, but practices skillful and compliant reflection; if one does not calculate "self" and "other," nor act with the entanglements of views or perversions, and remains free from ignorance and the like—this is called the cessation of afflictions, the absence of recollective thought, and ultimate subduing.
"O Son of Heaven! This is called ultimate subduing.

If a bodhisattva further uses wisdom to know that afflictions are thus minute, deceptive, and insubstantial; empty, without a master, without self, and without anything to which they belong; from whence they do not come, to where they do not go, and have no location; being neither internal, nor external, nor in between the two; not a accumulated thing; colorless, formless, signless, featureless, and without a place—then such afflictions are ultimately extinguished."
"O Devaputra!
It is like a person who, being able to recognize the species from which a venomous snake was born, is then able to neutralize its poison.
In the same way, O Devaputra!"
"If one knows that which is produced from the lineage of afflictions,
one can extinguish those afflictions. The devaputra said, "Mañjuśrī!"
"What is it that is produced from the seed-nature of afflictions? Mañjuśrī replied, "O Devaputra!"

Afflictions arise from deluded conceptualization; if there is no deluded conceptualization, then there are no afflictions. Because there are no afflictions, there is no cave of meditation; because there is no cave of meditation, there is no place of abiding. Because there is no place of abiding, there is no harm or vexation; because there is no harm or vexation, one attains ultimate subduing.
The devaputra said:
"Mañjuśrī, is it because of the existence of afflictions that there is subduing?"
"Is it for the sake of being free from afflictions that one is tamed? Mañjuśrī replied, "O Devaputra!"

It is like a person who dreams of being bitten by a venomous snake; tormented by this suffering, he immediately takes an antidote within the dream, and because he has taken the medicine, the toxic vapors are eliminated.
"Devaputra! What do you think?
Was this person truly bitten by a snake?"
The devaputra said, “No. Mañjuśrī said:
“Does that poison truly get eliminated? The devaputra said, “Mañjuśrī!
"Just as one who is not actually stung by a venomous insect is cured in the same way. Mañjuśrī said, "O Devaputra!"
The taming of all worthy and holy ones is likewise so.
O Son of Heaven!
You have spoken these words:
"Is it for the sake of those with afflictions that they are tamed, or for those without?
"O Devaputra! Just as there is 'self' and 'non-self,' so too it is with the presence or absence of afflictions."
Just as there is no self and yet no non-self, so too it is with the presence and absence of afflictions; for the self is itself the non-self.
Regarding the presence or absence of afflictions, there are no afflictions to be subdued here or anywhere else.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are quiescent, for they are not objects of attachment.
All phenomena are quiescent, for they cannot be grasped.
All phenomena are ultimately quiescent, because they cannot arise.
All phenomena are inexhaustible, because they do not arise.
All phenomena are unarisen, because they are not established.
All phenomena are without accomplishment, because there is no agent.
All phenomena have no self as an agent, because they are without self.
All phenomena are without self, because they are without a master.
All phenomena have no master, for they are equal to empty space.
All phenomena have no coming, for they have nothing upon which to rely.
All phenomena have no going, for they have no meditative cave.
All phenomena are without abiding, because they have no established foundation.
All phenomena are without establishment, because arising is itself cessation.
All phenomena are unconditioned, because they are untainted.
"All dharmas are without grasping, because they are ultimately tamed.
The Devaputra Śāntavighuṣṭaśvara then addressed the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, saying:
"What is the supreme among all dharmas?"
Mañjuśrī said: "Among the practices of saṃsāra, non-virtuous compliance is foremost;
for proceeding toward the realm of nirvāṇa, virtuous compliance is foremost."
Among obstacles, lack of diligence is foremost; among states of perfect awakening, diligence is foremost.
Among the hindrances, the net of doubt is foremost; among various signs, the attainment of liberating insight is foremost.
Among all afflictions, conceptual proliferation is the foremost; among the absence of afflictions, non-proliferation is the foremost.
Among all states of awakening, manifold activity is the foremost; for the mind that has entered cessation, meditative concentration is the foremost.
Among all views, overweening pride is the foremost; among all dharmas of emptiness, the absence of overweening pride is the foremost.
Among all unwholesome dharmas, the evil spiritual friend is the foremost; among all wholesome dharmas, the virtuous spiritual friend is the foremost.
Among all dharmas of suffering, false view is the foremost; among all dharmas of happiness, right view is the foremost.
Among the destitute, stinginess and greed are the foremost; among the great wealthy, generosity is the foremost.
Among the miserable realms, the breaking of precepts is foremost; among the superior realms, the upholding of precepts is foremost.
Within a defiled mind, anger is foremost; within a pure mind, patience is foremost.
Among those factors that cause one to fall away from wholesome qualities, laziness is the foremost; among those for cultivating wholesome qualities, diligence is the foremost.
Among states of distraction, discursive thoughts are the foremost; among states of single-mindedness, meditative concentration is the foremost.
Among the absence of wisdom, delusion is foremost; among the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, prajñā is foremost.

Within the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), non-obstruction is foremost; within the mind of compassion (*karuṇā*), single-minded mindfulness free from flattery is foremost; within the mind of sympathetic joy (*muditā*), delighting in the Dharma is foremost; and within the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*), being free from love and hatred is foremost.

Among the applications of mindfulness, not forgetting past roots of goodness is supreme; among the right efforts, correct skillful means is supreme; among the bases of psychic power, lightness of body and mind is supreme; among the faculties, faith is supreme; among the powers, subduing the afflictions is supreme; among the factors of enlightenment, awakening to equality is supreme; among the eightfold noble path, crossing over all deviant paths is supreme; and among the Buddha-dharmas, the bodhicitta is supreme.

Among the means of gathering [beings], material gifts and the Dharma are supreme; among the ways of guiding and transforming sentient beings, preaching the Dharma is supreme; and among skillful means, the knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible is supreme.

Within the *prajñāpāramitā*, knowing the continuous succession of the mental activities of all sentient beings and reaching the other shore is supreme; among the six *pāramitās*, the Mahāyāna is supreme.
"In seeking emptiness, the clarity of wisdom is supreme; in the renunciation through the patience toward dharmas, not relying on others is supreme.
The Devaputra Śāntavimalaghoṣa then addressed the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, saying: "Mañjuśrī!..."
"What constitutes the supreme within the dharma-realm? Mañjuśrī replied,
"O Son of Heaven!..."
"The Dharma-realm takes equality as its supreme quality. The Devaputra said: "Mañjuśrī!"
"What constitutes the boundary of the Dharma-realm? Mañjuśrī replied,
"The Dharma-realm takes the realm of all sentient beings as its boundary."
The devaputra said:
“Mañjuśrī! Does the dharma-realm have any boundaries or divisions?”
Mañjuśrī said: "Devaputra, what do you think?"
"Does the realm of space have any boundaries?
The devaputra replied, "It does not."
Mañjuśrī said: “Devaputra! Just as the realm of space has no boundaries, so too the dharma-realm has no boundaries.”
The devaputra said:
“Mañjuśrī! If the dharma-realm is thus, how do you, O Venerable One, know the dharma-realm?”
Mañjuśrī said: "The dharma-realm is itself the absence of a dharma-realm; the dharma-realm does not know the dharma-realm.
The devaputra said:
“Mañjuśrī! If it is so, what dharma do you know that your eloquence is such as this? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Son of Heaven! What do you think?
Does the sound of an echo know any dharma such that it responds to a call?”
The devaputra said:
“The resonance of a call has no cognition; it is only because of the conjunction of causes and conditions that sound arises. Mañjuśrī said:
"Thus it is, O Devaputra!
Because they take sentient beings as their objective sphere, the Bodhisattvas possess the eloquence of responsiveness.
The Devaputra said:
“Virtuous one, in what state do you abide when you preach the Dharma? Mañjuśrī replied, “Devaputra!”
"Just as the Dharma spoken by a transformation being created by the Tathāgata abides, so too is the Dharma I speak.
The devaputra said: "Mañjuśrī!..."
"Because that which is emanated by the Tathāgata has no abiding place, it nevertheless has something to be taught. Mañjuśrī said:
"I am also like this; because I have no abiding place, I nevertheless have something to be taught."
The devaputra said:
“Mañjuśrī! If there is no dwelling anywhere at all, in what place do you dwell to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”
Mañjuśrī said: “I shall abide in the Avīci hell and attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The devaputra said:
“Immediately thereafter, where does he abide? Mañjuśrī said,
“O Devaputra!...”
"Regarding 'the unintermittent' (ānantarya), it has no root and no place of abiding. The Devaputra said: "Mañjuśrī!"
“Does the Tathāgata not say that one who has accomplished the karma of immediate retribution will go to the Avīci hell? Mañjuśrī replied, “Devaputra!
"There is an action of immediate retribution (ānantarya-karman) which the Tathāgata says leads to the Avīci Hell.
In this way, O Devaputra!
A bodhisattva who abides in the five immediacies swiftly attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
What are these five?
If a bodhisattva, while single-mindedly recollecting and generating the mind set on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, does not fall into the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha in the interim.
Furthermore, when one relinquishes all that one possesses, during that interval one does not associate with a mind stained by stinginess.
Furthermore, thinking "I ought to save all sentient beings," during that interval one does not give rise to a base or inferior mind.
Furthermore, having realized that all phenomena are unarisen, one attains patience regarding the nature of arising; during this interval, one does not associate with various views.

Moreover, regarding that which should be known, seen, realized, and perfectly awakened to—all such things are perfectly awakened to through the skillful means and wisdom of a single mind and a single moment, until the attainment of omniscience, never becoming weary or negligent in the interim.
"O Son of Heaven!
These are called the five immediacies.
When a bodhisattva abides in these immediacies, they swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
The devaputra said: “Mañjuśrī!

Is it possible that an ordinary, foolish person who dwells in the state of an immediate transgression and is headed for the Avīci hell, while a bodhisattva likewise dwells in this same state of immediacy, can realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”
Mañjuśrī said: "There is. The devaputra asked:
"By what means? Mañjuśrī replied, "O Devaputra!

All phenomena are empty because the various sense bases (*āyatana*) are themselves empty; they are empty, signless, wishless, unarisen, unoriginated, unconditioned, and uncreated. Because they accord with dependent origination, they are *bodhi*.
The devaputra said:
"Mañjuśrī! This Dharma cannot be seen."
"Who would believe this? Mañjuśrī replied,
"If one does not have faith and compliance toward the Tathāgata, how could one possibly have faith in the śrāvakas?"
The devaputra asked,
"If this is so, how can one attain liberation? Mañjuśrī replied:

"If one does not act with self-interest; if one does not accept any afflictions; if one further upholds such a sutra as this; or if one bestows the hand of the Dharma upon all sentient beings through great compassion."
He asked, "What are their characteristics? He replied:
"They shall have the characteristics of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases.
He asked: "What conduct shall they have?"
He said: "One should practice emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. He asked:
"Where will they go? He replied, "They shall go toward omniscience; they shall go toward the mental activities of all sentient beings."
He asked: "Mañjuśrī! What is a bodhisattva who regresses?"
He said: "O Son of Heaven!
It is impossible for a regressive bodhisattva to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
He asked: "From what do they regress? He replied:
"Regarding all afflictions and the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas," he asked,
"What is meant by 'not falling back'?"
He said: "It is equal to equality. He asked:
“Mañjuśrī! What is the meaning of the phrase ‘equality’? He replied:
"This is the teaching of non-differentiation. He said: "Mañjuśrī!..."
"If it is thus, how does one know the distinctions among all phenomena?
He replied, "O Devaputra!..."
Those who do not know equality give rise to differentiation within equality; because they practice differentiation, they proceed toward differentiation.
Those who know equality do not practice differentiation; because they do not practice differentiation, they proceed toward equality—that is, they proceed toward non-differentiation.
The devaputra said:
"Mañjuśrī! Is there any bodhisattva who possesses afflictions and yet possesses awakening?"
He replied, "There are. He asked again:
"By what skillful means? Mañjuśrī replied,
"If a bodhisattva were free from afflictions like a śrāvaka, they would not undergo rebirth."
"O Son of Heaven!

Because a bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion and awakens the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta) for the sake of severing the afflictions of all sentient beings, it is said that there is 'bodhi'. "Mañjuśrī! [the King asked.]
"Is there perhaps a bodhisattva who possesses both stinginess and awakening? He replied, "There is."
The devaputra asked, "By what skillful means? Mañjuśrī replied:

"If a bodhisattva, without abandoning the bodhicitta, transforms and delivers sentient beings while gathering and upholding all dharmas, this bodhisattva possesses stinginess yet accomplishes the dāna-pāramitā."
The devaputra said:
“Mañjuśrī! Is there any bodhisattva who, having relinquished the precepts, nonetheless accomplishes the śīlapāramitā?”
He replied, "There is. The Son of Heaven said:
“By what means? Mañjuśrī replied,

“If a bodhisattva acts for the sake of sentient beings in order to transform and deliver them, that bodhisattva is one who, without a formal precept, achieves the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā).”
The devaputra said:
“Mañjuśrī! Is there any bodhisattva who abandons patience yet still accomplishes the pāramitā of kṣānti?”
He replied, "There is. The Son of Heaven said:
“By what means? Mañjuśrī replied,

“If a bodhisattva relinquishes all patience regarding heterodox paths and cultivates the patience of the Buddha-dharma, this bodhisattva’s relinquishment of patience brings about the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).”
The devaputra said:
"Mañjuśrī! Is there any bodhisattva who abandons diligence yet accomplishes the *vīrya-pāramitā*?"
He replied, "There is. The Son of Heaven said:
“By what means? Mañjuśrī replied,

“If a bodhisattva abandons the diligence of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas to advance toward the enlightenment of equal and perfect awakening (samyaksaṃbodhi), this bodhisattva abandons [ordinary] diligence and accomplishes the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā).”
The devaputra said:
“Mañjuśrī! Is it possible for a bodhisattva who has lost mindfulness to achieve the dhyānapāramitā?”
He replied, "There is. The Son of Heaven said:
“By what skillful means? Mañjuśrī replied,

“If a bodhisattva does not give rise to thoughts of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas even in dreams, and remains constantly settled without abandoning the mind of equal and perfect enlightenment, this bodhisattva accomplishes the dhyāna-pāramitā through the perfection of mindfulness.”
The devaputra said:
"Mañjuśrī! Is there any bodhisattva who, lacking wisdom, achieves the perfection of prajñā?"
He replied, "There is. The Son of Heaven said:
“By what skillful means? Mañjuśrī replied, “If a bodhisattva,

regarding all worldly sorcery, the raising of corpses, and various evil incantations, possesses no wisdom therein, but practices them solely for the sake of accomplishing the gathering of all-knowledge, then this bodhisattva, through the absence of such [worldly] wisdom, accomplishes the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).”
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, saying: “Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī!”
You have well explained what a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice and what they should not practice.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī,
I shall now speak a parable for you to further clarify this meaning.
Mañjuśrī! Suppose there were a person who was emaciated by hunger and thirst; that person would rather endure their hunger and thirst than ever eat food mixed with poison. Why is this?
Because food is something to be feared. In this way, Mañjuśrī,
a bodhisattva would rather be stingy, envious, immoral, ill-reputed, lazy, forgetful, and lacking wisdom than ever seek the stage of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.
"Why is this? Because it is fearsome.
The devaputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Are the bodhisattvas not afraid of the afflictions?
The Buddha told the devaputra:
"One should fear the afflictions; yet the fear of the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas exceeds even that.
Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!
I now ask you; answer according to your own understanding."
"Son of Heaven!
What do you think?
Of what should a person who seeks birth be afraid—of having their head cut off, or of having their limbs severed?"
The devaputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I am afraid of having my head cut off.”

Why is this? One who has their limbs severed can still cultivate meritorious deeds and be reborn in a superior realm; however, one whose head is severed possesses no life-force and is thus unable to cultivate merit.
The Buddha told the devaputra: “It is so.
A bodhisattva would rather violate the prohibitive precepts than ever abandon right view; he would rather possess afflictions than ever ascend to the fixed stage of a śrāvaka.”
The devaputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!
That which the bodhisattvas practice is difficult for the world to believe.”
"Why is this? For the śrāvaka who upholds the precepts and exerts diligence, that very conduct constitutes a bodhisattva’s breaking of the precepts and indolence.
The Buddha told the devaputra:
"As you have said, O Devaputra, just as a poor man’s food would be poison to a Wheel-Turning King,
so too is the precept-keeping and diligence of a śrāvaka the breaking of precepts and indolence of a bodhisattva."
"O Son of Heaven!
It is like a person who lives by manual labor; such a person cannot even provide for his own family and dependents to bring them happiness, let alone others."
Thus it is, O Devaputra!
The diligence of a śrāvaka is for the sake of severing his own fetters; by means of this diligence, he cannot bring happiness to the people of Jambudvīpa, much less to all others.
"Son of Heaven!
Just as a great caravan leader who possesses abundant wealth and treasures, constantly delights in providing relief and aid with tireless diligence, is thus able to benefit all sentient beings."
Thus it is, O Devaputra!

When a bodhisattva, with single-minded diligence, accomplishes compassion, they are able to benefit all sentient beings, acting as a cause of happiness for immeasurable beings, and capable of bestowing both worldly and supramundane bliss.
At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Śrāvakas realize unconditioned dharmas, whereas Bodhisattvas reach the conditioned.”
"Regarding those who have reached the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), how can one disparage those who have reached the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"I shall provide you with a parable to clarify this meaning."

Kāśyapa! It is like the four great oceans filled with clarified butter; suppose a person were to split a single hair into one hundred parts and, with one part of that hair, take up a single drop of the butter.
Kāśyapa! What do you think?
Could a single drop from the tip of a hair outweigh the clarified butter filling the four oceans?
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
It cannot be taken lightly."
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:
"What do you think? Of these two kinds of ghee, which is more?"
"What is it that is of such high value?
Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"A single drop of butter produced from one great ocean is already more and superior than a hundred thousand billionth part [of it], let alone that of the four oceans. Kāśyapa,
you should know that the unconditioned wisdom of the śrāvakas is likewise like a single drop of butter raised by one hair-tip out of a hundred."

Kāśyapa! Just as butter is produced from the four great oceans, you should know that the dedication of a bodhisattva’s conditioned roots of goodness toward omniscience over hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya kalpas is likewise so.
Kāśyapa! It is like an ant taking a single grain of rice and comparing it to all the grains upon the entire earth when the autumn harvest has ripened. Kāśyapa!
"What do you think?
Of these two kinds of grain, which one is more abundant and superior?
Kāśyapa replied to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
When the autumn moon reaches its fullness, immeasurable sentient beings each obtain its enjoyment;
this is most excellent. “It is so, Kāśyapa!”
Just as an ant takes up a single grain of rice, one should know that the fruit of liberation of a śrāvaka is likewise.

Kāśyapa, just as all the crops upon the great earth ripen in the autumn month, one should know that when a bodhisattva has brought to maturity the roots of goodness of the six pāramitās and the four means of attraction, they are then able to benefit immeasurable sentient beings; it is just so.
Kāśyapa! It is like hundreds of thousands of loads of crystal vessels entering a city;

yet there is also a priceless lapis lazuli jewel, which, having been carried upon a ship across the great ocean, arrives safely within the realm of Jambudvīpa, and once arrived, is able to eliminate the suffering of poverty and destitution for all people.
Kāśyapa! What do you think?
Could various vessels made of crystal possibly outweigh this priceless lapis lazuli jewel?
Kāśyapa said to the Buddha, “I would not dare to treat them lightly. “Kāśyapa! [the Buddha replied.]
Just as when crystal enters a city or town, one should know that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) of the śrāvaka is likewise.

Just as with a priceless great jewel of lapis lazuli, one should know that the bodhisattva’s succession of the three jewels so as not to let them be severed, and the production of the jewel-mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*), are likewise.
At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata has spoken excellently!”
"A single jewel-like mind of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) in a bodhisattva surpasses all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
At that time, the bodhisattvas who had come from the land of the Tathāgata Ratnākara, having heard this teaching, were all filled with wonder and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
All that has been said here is mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), giving rise to various impure and pure divergent doctrines.
In the buddha-field of that Tathāgata Ratnākara, only the Dharma of the non-retrogressive bodhisattvas is taught, and there is no entanglement of afflictions (*kleśa*).
How rare and difficult to equal!

Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, is indeed able to endure such afflictions as these, and within the non-conceptual, single-flavor Dharma, he teaches of superior, middling, and inferior capacities, manifesting the distinctions between the three vehicles.
At that time, after the bodhisattvas had made offerings to the Tathāgata with various celestial flowers, they addressed the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, saying: “Mañjuśrī!
"We wish to return to the world of Ratnāvatī. Mañjuśrī said,
"O sons of good family!..."
"You should know that now is the time. The bodhisattvas said,
"Will you not go together with us, O Benevolent One?"
Mañjuśrī said: “Good son! In the state where buddha-fields are equal, and where the Buddha-dharma and sentient beings are equal, I desire this and shall proceed to that place.”
The bodhisattvas said: "Mañjuśrī! By what skillful means?"

Mañjuśrī said: "Because all buddha-fields are equal and inexhaustible, the Buddhas, the Truly and Fully Enlightened Ones, are inconceivable; all phenomena are empty, and the self-nature of sentient beings is without self."
"Sons of good family!
I contemplate the nature of equality in this way, and therefore I speak thus: because all buddha-fields are equal and all buddha-dharmas and sentient beings are equal, I proceed toward that state."

Thereupon, Mañjuśrī entered into samādhi and transformed this world so that it became like the world-system Ratnāvatī; the entire great assembly clearly beheld it without increase or decrease, and they also saw the World-Honored One Śākyamuni’s countenance and physical form as being identical to those of the Tathāgata Ratnaketu, while all the śrāvaka followers appeared with the same complexions, forms, and features as those bodhisattvas.

At that time, having seen these signs, those bodhisattvas all thought they had already arrived in the world-system of Ratnāvatī; they all considered Śākyamuni Buddha to be the Tathāgata Ratnaketu and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"Who will bring us back to this world?
The Buddha told the bodhisattvas:
"O sons of good family!"
He asked, "When you departed, who led you away?
The bodhisattvas replied, "The Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī."
The Buddha told the bodhisattvas,
"He will also return.
At that time, Mañjuśrī emerged from samādhi and said to the bodhisattvas:
“Good sons! Each of you should contemplate samādhi.
Then, after each of the bodhisattvas had contemplated it and the samādhi they had attained had manifested before them, they thought this:
"How rare, how rare!
While we are still here, we say that we have already arrived at the world of Jewel-Abode.
At that time, the bodhisattvas, marveling at such an unprecedented occurrence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How extraordinary, World-Honored One!
Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, is truly capable of such inconceivable power of supernormal knowledge and concentration.
World-Honored One!"
"May all sentient beings attain supernatural powers such as those of Mañjuśrī.
The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying,
"O sons of noble family!"
It is, for example, like various vessels made of gold, silver, crystal, diamond, sandalwood, and so forth, as well as vessels made of clay; all such vessels alike contain the space-element.
The space-element pervades all vessels because the space-element is equal.
In this same way, noble sons!

Whether it be dharmas, suchness, the limit, or emptiness—these various dharmas are entirely without distinction, for they enter into the ultimate emptiness of the primary meaning (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).

Because those sentient beings perform various kinds of actions, they undergo various births and manifest a thousandfold self, differentiating and transforming into thousands of forms: the forms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas; and the forms of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas.
Although all these forms are visible, they are equal; their suchness and their emptiness are one and the same, without distinction or difference.
O sons of good family!
"For this reason, you should understand it thus.
Mañjuśrī, the Prince of Dharma, said:
"Because all buddha-fields are equal and without distinction, all Buddhas are equal, all dharmas are equal, and all sentient beings are equal, being without differentiation."

Then those bodhisattvas, having received the World-Honored One’s teaching in accordance with the Dharma, gave rise to a profound sense of weary detachment and felt joy in their hearts; they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and circumambulated him three times to the right.
Having departed from the World-Honored One, he immediately vanished from the Sahā world and returned to the Ratnavyūha world.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying: “Ānanda!
You should receive, uphold, read, recite, and extensively master this supreme sūtra.
Why is this? If one can widely expound this sūtra for others, or if one intentionally listens to and receives it, one will obtain an immeasurable mass of merit.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So be it, World-Honored One!
I have received and upheld it."
"What should this sutra be named?
How should it be upheld?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This sutra shall be known by the title 'The Questions of Śāntasvarā'; thus should it be upheld.
It may also be called 'The Pure Discipline Spoken and Upheld by the Tathāgata.'"

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Devaputra Śāntasvararāja, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, the Elder Mahākāśyapa, the Venerable Ānanda, and the great assembly gathered at that time—including devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, and world-protectors—having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Sūtra on the Questions of Śāntamati (Śāntamatinirdeśa-sūtra)
